title: Mardi Gras Hangover Survival Guide: Pace, Hydrate, Recover
excerpt: How to enjoy Mardi Gras without losing Ash Wednesday: pacing a long parade day, go-cups and big cocktails, hydration with long bathroom lines, food, safety, and recovery.
metaDescription: Mardi Gras survival guide: pace a long parade day, handle go-cups and big cocktails, stay hydrated, eat right, stay safe, and recover on Ash Wednesday.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Mardi Gras is hard on your body not because of one big night, but because it stacks the things that cause bad hangovers on top of each other. You're drinking outside for many hours, often starting before noon, from big cups that hold more than they look like they do, with long bathroom lines that tempt you to skip water, crowds that make it hard to eat a real meal, and very little sleep. Most people who feel wrecked on Ash Wednesday didn't do anything unusual. They just did all of those things at once, sometimes for several days in a row.

**The quick rules:** Eat a real breakfast before the first drink. Set a pace you can hold for the whole day, roughly one drink an hour or slower, and treat the big souvenir-cup cocktails as two or three drinks, not one. Match every drink with water, and plan your bathroom stops instead of drinking less water to avoid them. Eat again at lunch and dinner. Pick an end time before you start. Have a ride home sorted out in advance, and never drive. This guide is for adults 21 and older, which is Louisiana's legal drinking age.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and practical guidance. It isn't a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Call 911 if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, is vomiting while passed out, or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." **See a doctor if you** can't keep fluids down for many hours, are vomiting blood, have severe belly or chest pain, feel confused, or are getting worse after 24 hours instead of better. If you drank heavily for several days in a row and then develop shaking, heavy sweating, a racing heart, or hallucinations after stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal and needs medical care.

## Why Mardi Gras Hangovers Hit So Hard

A hangover is your body reacting to a mix of problems that alcohol causes at once. Researchers still debate which piece matters most, but the usual suspects are well known: poor sleep, dehydration and lost electrolytes, an irritated stomach, low blood sugar, inflammation, and a by-product of alcohol breakdown called acetaldehyde. Mardi Gras happens to make almost every one of these worse.

**The day is long.** Parades can run for hours, and many people arrive early to claim a spot. A long drinking window means more total alcohol, even if each individual drink feels modest. Your liver clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate, around one standard drink per hour for an average adult, and nothing you eat or drink speeds that up much. If you drink faster than that for ten hours, the extra piles up.

**The cups are big.** Many of the famous New Orleans drinks come in tall plastic cups, and some of the rum-heavy cocktails sold in the French Quarter are strong as well as large. One of those can hold the equivalent of several standard drinks. People who think "I had four drinks" have often had closer to ten.

**You skip water on purpose.** Restrooms along parade routes are limited, the lines are long, and many bars and restaurants reserve their bathrooms for paying customers. A lot of people respond by drinking less water so they don't have to go. That's the opposite of what helps.

**Meals get lost.** It's easy to snack on fried food and king cake all day without ever eating a real meal. Alcohol absorbs faster on an empty stomach, and you end the night with low blood sugar.

**Sleep is short and broken.** Late night on Frenchmen or Bourbon Street, early start for the next parade, a hotel or rental full of people. Alcohol already makes sleep lighter and more broken in the second half of the night, so short sleep plus drinking is a bad pair.

**It's often several days in a row.** Carnival season starts on January 6 (Twelfth Night), and the parade calendar gets dense in the final two weekends before Fat Tuesday. Visitors frequently come for a long weekend that runs straight into Mardi Gras day itself. Each morning you start a little more behind than the last.

**The weather varies.** February in New Orleans can be chilly and damp one year and warm and humid the next. Warm sun and crowds mean sweating, which adds to fluid loss. Cold, wet weather means you may not feel thirsty, so you drink less water without noticing.

## New Orleans Specifics You Should Know

If you've never been to Mardi Gras, a few local rules and habits change how you should plan.

### Go-cups and open containers

New Orleans is known for letting people carry drinks on the street, as long as they're in plastic or paper cups rather than glass or cans that could break. Bars will pour your drink into a "go-cup" when you leave. This is part of what makes the day so easy to drink through: there's no natural pause between bars, and you can always be holding a drink. Rules can vary by area and change over time, so follow what you see posted and what police tell you on the day.

The practical takeaway is that the drink in your hand never runs out on its own. You have to decide when it does. A simple habit is to carry a refillable water bottle (where allowed) or buy bottled water and keep it in the other hand, so you always have something to sip that isn't alcohol.

### No glass on the parade route

The city prohibits glass containers along parade routes during Carnival, mainly because broken glass in a dense crowd is dangerous. Plan on plastic for everything, including any water or mixers you bring.

### Parade routes, krewes, and long waits

Parades are put on by social clubs called krewes, and the big ones roll on set routes through Uptown and into downtown, with smaller and more irreverent parades in the Marigny and French Quarter. Families with kids often line St. Charles Avenue, while the Quarter skews more toward adult partying. Either way, expect to stand or sit in one place for a long time. That's when people drink out of boredom. Bring snacks, a chair if you're staking out a spot, and something to do between floats.

### Bathrooms

This is the single most practical thing to plan. Portable toilets exist along many routes, and some businesses sell restroom access for the day, but lines can be long. Before you set up, figure out where your nearest options are. If you're staying close to the route, a quick trip back to your room can save a long wait. Knowing where you'll go makes it much easier to keep drinking water.

### Getting around

Streets close for parades, traffic is heavy, and rideshare prices often spike and pickups get slow near the routes. Many people walk long distances, so wear shoes you can stand in for ten hours. Agree on a meeting spot with your group in case phones die or you get separated, and keep your phone charged with a small battery pack. If you drove into town, leave the car parked until you're fully sober, which is often much later than you think.

## The Mardi Gras Day Drinking Plan

Our general [day drinking guide](/never-hungover/day-drinking) covers the basics of starting early. Here's how to apply them to a parade day in New Orleans. For crowded, all-night celebrations in general, our [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips) cover pacing and getting home safely.

### The night before

- **Get to bed at a reasonable hour.** If you're going out the night before a big parade day, cut it off earlier than you would at home. You'll thank yourself at the 11 a.m. parade.
- **Lay out what you need.** Water bottle, phone battery, cash, sunscreen, a light layer, and anything you plan to use the next day. A small "survival kit" in a cross-body bag keeps your hands free. Our [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) list has a good starting point.
- **Drink water before bed.** Start the day well hydrated rather than trying to catch up.

### Morning: build a base

- **Eat a real breakfast.** Protein, fat, and carbohydrates, such as eggs with toast and grits, or a breakfast sandwich. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol enters your blood. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes deeper.
- **Start with water, not a drink.** Have a big glass of water or an electrolyte drink before the first cocktail.
- **Hold off on the first drink.** Starting at 10 a.m. means a much longer day than starting at 1 p.m. If the parade you care about is in the evening, there's no rule that says you have to begin at breakfast.

### Midday: set the pace

- **Count in standard drinks, not cups.** In the US, a standard drink is about 14 grams of alcohol: roughly a 12-ounce beer at 5%, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. A large rum cocktail with several shots in it counts as several drinks.
- **Pick lower-strength drinks for the long middle stretch.** Light beer, a beer with a seltzer in between, or a wine spritzer spreads the same "always holding something" feeling over less alcohol. Save the famous strong cocktail for a moment you'll actually enjoy it, and have just one.
- **Alternate every drink with water.** One alcoholic drink, one water. It slows you down and keeps you hydrated.
- **Eat lunch.** Not just a bag of chips. Po'boys, red beans and rice, jambalaya, or anything with real substance. Stop for it even if the parade is rolling.

### Afternoon: the danger zone

This is where most people get into trouble. You've been drinking for several hours, you feel fine, the crowd is getting louder, and it's easy to speed up.

- **Check in with yourself every hour.** How many drinks so far? When did you last have water? When did you last eat?
- **Take a real break.** Sit down somewhere with shade or warmth, drink water, eat something, and skip a round. Twenty or thirty minutes off can reset the whole evening.
- **Watch out for shots.** Shots handed around in a group add alcohol fast and are easy to lose count of.

### Evening: land the plane

- **Set your end time in advance.** Decide before you start when your last drink will be. A good rule is to stop alcohol at least a couple of hours before you plan to sleep.
- **Eat dinner.** A full meal before your last drink helps.
- **Switch to water for the walk home.** The go-cup can hold water just as easily.
- **Sort out the ride.** Rideshare can be slow and expensive, so plan for it. Walking alone late at night after heavy drinking isn't a good idea; stay with your group.

## Pacing Math: How a Mardi Gras Day Adds Up

It helps to see how fast the numbers move. These are rough examples, not exact counts, because drink sizes and strengths vary a lot from bar to bar.

| Scenario | What it looks like | Rough standard drinks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steady and slow | 1 beer an hour for 8 hours, water in between | about 8 |
| Mixed day | 4 beers, 2 mixed drinks, 1 big rum cocktail | about 9 to 11 |
| Souvenir-cup day | 3 big strong cocktails plus a few beers | can easily be 12 or more |

Even the "steady and slow" day is a lot of alcohol. The point isn't that any of these is safe. It's that the big cups make it very easy to drink twice what you think you have. If you want a lower total, the most effective moves are starting later, choosing smaller and lighter drinks, and stopping earlier.

## Hydration and Electrolytes on Parade Day

Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Over a long day outside, especially in sun or humidity, that adds up. Our article on [how alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains the mechanism in more detail.

What works in practice:

- **Water between every drink.** This is the most useful single habit.
- **An electrolyte drink or two during the day.** Sports drinks, oral rehydration drinks, or electrolyte powders mixed into a water bottle can help replace the salt you lose through sweat and urine. You don't need these all day; plain water covers most of it.
- **Salty food.** Many classic New Orleans dishes are already well salted, which helps you hold onto fluid.
- **Don't wait until you're thirsty.** In a loud crowd with a drink in your hand, thirst is easy to miss.
- **Plan bathrooms rather than rationing water.** Rationing water is the most common Mardi Gras hydration mistake.

For the morning after, our guide to [rehydrating after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) walks through what to drink and how fast.

## Food Strategy: Eat Like a Local, Not Like a Snacker

New Orleans has some of the best food in the country, and Mardi Gras is a great excuse to eat it. The trick is to eat real meals at regular times, not just graze.

- **Breakfast:** eggs, grits, biscuits, a breakfast po'boy. Something with protein and fat.
- **Lunch:** a po'boy, red beans and rice, gumbo, jambalaya. Rice and bread give you slow carbohydrates; meat, beans, and seafood add protein.
- **Snacks between:** bring something portable, like nuts, crackers, a sandwich, or fruit, so you aren't relying on whatever is closest when you get hungry.
- **King cake:** fine as a treat, but sugar alone won't hold you up for hours.
- **Dinner:** sit down for it if you can. A real meal before the evening parades or the late-night stretch makes a big difference.

Eating doesn't stop alcohol from reaching your blood. It slows the rate, which lowers your peak level and gives your liver more time.

## Looking Out for Your Group

Mardi Gras crowds are huge, and it's easy for one person in a group to get into trouble without anyone noticing. A few simple agreements help:

- **Use a buddy system.** Nobody wanders off alone, especially after dark.
- **Agree on a meeting spot.** Pick a specific corner or landmark in case people get separated or phones die.
- **Watch your drink.** Keep it in your hand, and don't accept open drinks from strangers.
- **Know the warning signs of alcohol poisoning.** Confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, pale or bluish skin, seizures, or not being able to wake someone up. If you see these, call 911. Our [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) guide covers what to do while you wait. Don't let someone who is very drunk "sleep it off" alone, and if they're passed out, roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit.
- **Respect your limits.** It's completely normal to sit out a round, switch to water, or head back early. Nobody at Mardi Gras is keeping score.

If you or someone in your group doesn't drink, or is choosing not to on a given day, the parades, food, music, and throws are a full experience on their own. Plenty of locals bring kids to the family-friendly stretches of the routes and drink little or nothing.

## Multi-Day Mardi Gras: Surviving a Long Weekend

If you're in town for several days, think of it as a trip, not a single party.

- **Choose your big days.** Pick the one or two nights you most want to go hard, and keep the others lighter. Not every parade has to be a drinking event.
- **Protect at least one good night of sleep.** Even one early night in the middle can make the back half of the trip far more enjoyable.
- **Start each day with water and food.** Before any thought of a drink.
- **Take an alcohol-free stretch.** A morning or afternoon off, maybe a walk through the Garden District, a museum, or a long lunch, lets your body catch up.
- **Watch for warning signs that you're overdoing it.** If you're waking up shaky, can't eat, or feel you need a drink to steady yourself in the morning, that's a signal to stop drinking for the rest of the trip, and if symptoms like shaking, sweating, or a racing heart get worse after you stop, see a doctor.

If Mardi Gras is one of several big events on your calendar, our list of the [biggest drinking days of the year](/never-hungover/biggest-drinking-days-of-the-year) has planning tips for the rest of them.

## The Morning After: Ash Wednesday Recovery

If you wake up hungover, there's no instant cure. The goal is to support your body while it does the work.

1. **Drink fluids slowly.** Water, an electrolyte drink, or broth. Sip rather than gulp if your stomach is upset.
2. **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, eggs, rice, bananas, or soup. Many people find that a real meal, once they can manage it, helps a lot.
3. **Rest.** Sleep is the most underrated hangover treatment. If you can, sleep in or nap.
4. **Choose a pain reliever carefully.** If you need one for a headache, ibuprofen or naproxen taken with food is a common choice, but they can irritate the stomach, which alcohol already does. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver and is best avoided after a very heavy night, especially if you drink heavily on a regular basis. Our comparison of [Advil vs. Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) explains the trade-offs. Follow label doses, and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines.
5. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink may delay how bad you feel, but it doesn't fix anything. It just pushes the hangover later.
6. **Don't drive until you're sure you're sober.** If you drank heavily until late, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, sometimes enough to be over the legal limit. Your flight or drive home can wait a few hours.

Most hangovers clear within about 24 hours. If you're getting worse instead of better, can't keep fluids down, or have any of the warning signs in the box at the top of this page, see a doctor.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that many people take around drinking. It's worth being clear about what's known:

- **Most of the research is in animals and lab studies.** Those studies looked at how DHM affects alcohol metabolism, the liver, and the brain's response to alcohol. Human data are limited, and there's no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people the way some marketing claims.
- **It doesn't lower your blood alcohol in a way you can rely on.** It won't make you safe to drive, and it isn't a reason to drink more.
- **It's not a substitute for the basics.** Food, pacing, water, and sleep do much more for how you'll feel on Ash Wednesday than any supplement.

If you want to try DHM as part of your routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when. If you take prescription medicines or have a health condition, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## A Simple Mardi Gras Packing List

- Refillable plastic water bottle (no glass) or cash for bottled water
- Electrolyte packets
- Portable snacks
- Phone battery pack and charging cable
- Cash and a card in a secure pocket or cross-body bag
- Sunscreen and sunglasses, plus a light layer for the evening chill
- Comfortable shoes you can stand in all day
- Hand sanitizer and tissues for portable toilets
- A small bag for the beads and throws you'll collect
- Your ride plan and your group's meeting spot

## The Bottom Line

The best Mardi Gras is one you remember. Eat real meals, drink water between every drink, treat the big cups as the multiple drinks they are, plan your bathroom stops, pick an end time, and get home safely. If you're staying for several days, choose your big nights and keep the rest lighter. Do those things and Ash Wednesday becomes a slow, lazy recovery day instead of a lost one.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you survive Mardi Gras without a bad hangover?**

Eat a real breakfast before your first drink, pace yourself at roughly one standard drink an hour or slower, drink water between every drink, and eat lunch and dinner instead of only snacking. Treat the big souvenir-cup cocktails as several drinks, plan your bathroom stops so you don't skip water, pick an end time in advance, and get some sleep. Nothing guarantees you won't be hungover, but these habits make the biggest difference.

**Can you drink on the street in New Orleans during Mardi Gras?**

New Orleans generally allows adults 21 and older to carry drinks outdoors in plastic or paper cups, often called go-cups, but not in glass. Glass containers are prohibited along parade routes during Carnival. Rules can vary by area and change over time, so follow posted signs and instructions from police on the day.

**How many drinks is a Hurricane or other big New Orleans cocktail?**

It depends on the bar, but many of the famous rum cocktails come in large cups and contain several shots of liquor, so a single one can equal two, three, or more standard drinks. A US standard drink is about 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. If you want to keep your total down, have one of the strong cocktails as a treat and switch to beer, wine spritzers, or water afterward.

**What should I eat before and during Mardi Gras drinking?**

Start with a breakfast that has protein, fat, and carbohydrates, like eggs with grits and toast or a breakfast sandwich. Then eat real meals at lunch and dinner, such as po'boys, red beans and rice, gumbo, or jambalaya, and carry portable snacks like nuts or crackers. Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. King cake is fine as a treat but won't hold you for long on its own.

**How do I stay hydrated at Mardi Gras with long bathroom lines?**

Plan where you'll go before you set up: portable toilets along the route, businesses that sell restroom access, or your hotel if it's close. Then drink a glass of water between every alcoholic drink and have an electrolyte drink or two during the day. Rationing water to avoid bathroom lines is one of the most common reasons people feel terrible the next morning.

**How do I get over a Mardi Gras hangover on Ash Wednesday?**

There's no instant cure. Sip water, an electrolyte drink, or broth, eat something gentle like toast, eggs, or soup, and rest as much as you can. If you need a pain reliever, ibuprofen with food is a common choice, though it can irritate the stomach; acetaminophen is best avoided after a very heavy night. Skip more alcohol, and don't drive until you're sure the alcohol has cleared. Most hangovers ease within about 24 hours.

**When should I get medical help after drinking at Mardi Gras?**

Call 911 if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, pale, or bluish skin. See a doctor if you can't keep fluids down, are vomiting blood, have severe belly or chest pain, feel confused, or are getting worse after 24 hours. Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or hallucinations after several days of heavy drinking can be alcohol withdrawal, which also needs medical care.

**Does DHM prevent Mardi Gras hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people use it as part of their routine, but it doesn't lower blood alcohol in a way you can rely on and isn't a substitute for eating, pacing, drinking water, and sleeping. Check with your doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicines.
